Abstract
In view of the problem that the high noise and data redundancy in the voiceprint 
signal of the wind turbine blade lead to insufficient diagnostic accuracy and real-
time performance and increase the acquisition cost, this paper combines sparse 
representation, compressed sensing, and deep learning technology to apply a new 
wind turbine blade damage detection method, aiming to enhance the accuracy 
and real-time performance of wind turbine blade damage diagnosis. The sparse 
representation method is used to effectively encode the voiceprint signal and extract 
representative signal features; the compressed sensing technology is applied to 
efficiently reconstruct the signal using a small amount of sampled data, significantly 
reducing the data collection amount and storage requirements; deep feature 
learning and damage pattern classification based on convolutional neural network 
further improve the accuracy and intelligence level of detection.The research results 
show that the proposed method effectively reduces the computational complexity 
and greatly improves the detection accuracy. The accuracy is not less than 88% 
under five damage types: crack, corrosion, deformation, fatigue and impact. It has 
good adaptability under different computing resources, and the processing delay 
does not exceed 0.45s under complex environments and large data volumes. It has 
strong real-time performance and application potential.
Highlights
  •  Innovative Fusion Approach: Combines sparse representation for feature 
encoding, compressed sensing for efficient data reconstruction, and deep 
learning (CNN) for intelligent damage classification, enhancing accuracy and real-
time performance in blade damage detection.
  •  High Accuracy & Efficiency: Achieves ≥ 88%  accuracy across five damage types 
(crack, corrosion, deformation, fatigue, impact) with processing delays ≤ 0.45s, 
even in complex environments and large datasets.
  •  Resource Adaptability: Demonstrates robust performance under varying 
computational resources, reducing data acquisition/storage costs while 
maintaining reliability in noisy, high-redundancy signal environments.

1  Introduction
As the wind energy industry develops rapidly, the scale of wind turbine use continues to 
expand. The health of wind turbine blades directly affects the stability and efficiency of 
wind power generation [1, 2]. As the core component of wind turbines, damage to wind 
turbine blades may lead to reduced operating efficiency and even cause system failure, 
resulting in huge economic losses [3, 4]. Damage to wind turbine blades not only affects 
power output, but may also lead to long-term equipment shutdown and increase mainte­
nance costs. Therefore, timely and accurate monitoring of wind turbine blade damage has 
essential practical significance and application value [5, 6]. Traditional wind turbine blade 
damage detection methods rely on high-cost sensors, complex signal acquisition systems, 
and large amounts of data processing, and these methods usually require manual interven­
tion or long signal processing time [7, 8]. In addition, these traditional methods are easily 
interfered by environmental noise, resulting in unstable detection results and the inability 
to achieve real-time and effective fault diagnosis [9, 10]. In a test at a certain wind farm, 
when using traditional vibration monitoring methods to diagnose blade damage, the sig­
nal fluctuations caused by wind speed fluctuations made it impossible for the system to 
accurately distinguish between normal vibration and damage signals. Experimental data 
showed that when the wind speed was high, the false alarm rate of traditional vibration 
sensors reached 15%, significantly affecting the accuracy of the monitoring results.There­
fore, how to design an efficient, low-cost, automated wind turbine blade damage detection 
technology that can cope with complex working conditions has become a hot topic in cur­
rent research [11, 12].
At present, many researchers have proposed different methods for wind turbine blade 
damage detection [13, 14]. Huang et al. [15] put forward a new image recognition tech­
nology that used the spectrum image of the vibration signal for vibration-based fault 
diagnosis. However, this method was highly sensitive to complex environmental noise 
and had difficulty coping with the dynamic changes of wind turbine blades under dif­
ferent working conditions. In addition, damage detection based on voiceprint signals 
gradually gained widespread attention. This method could detect the health of blades 
by analyzing the sound wave signals generated by the wind turbine during operation 
[16, 17]. As the feature signal of the wind turbine blade, the voiceprint signal has strong 
sensitivity and operability and can provide effective damage information [18, 19]. How­
ever, the voiceprint signal usually has a high dimension and information redundancy, 
and is easily affected by noise, resulting in difficulties in the signal processing process 
[20, 21]. Ogaili et al. [22] recognized various faults of wind turbine blades from the col­
lected vibration signals and calculated features based on the time domain vibration fea­
tures, aiming to extract key information, reduce the amount of data, and improve the 
reconstruction quality and processing efficiency of the signal. Although these methods 
have improved the signal processing effect to a certain extent, since the extraction and 
analysis of signal features still rely on manual intervention, there are still certain defi­
ciencies in their automation level and accuracy [23]. Numerous studies have focused on 
the application of machine learning technology in wind power systems. Khan et al. [24]

reviewed machine learning technologies used for fault detection, diagnosis, and predic­
tion in wind turbines. Research indicates that machine learning models can effectively 
improve the accuracy and efficiency of fault identification, reduce operational costs, and 
enhance system reliability. However, existing methods still face challenges such as dif­
ficulty in feature extraction and insufficient model generalization capabilities when deal­
ing with high-dimensional, complex wind turbine blade acoustic signature signals.
To further improve the accuracy, intelligence level, and automation capability of wind 
turbine blade damage detection, the application of deep learning (DL) technology in this 
field has gradually increased [25, 26]. Many researchers have automatically extracted fea­
tures from a large number of wind turbine voiceprint signals by using DL models such as 
convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks, and realized the 
classification and diagnosis of wind turbine blade damage [27, 28]. DL models can auto­
matically learn the deep features of signals based on training data, without relying on 
manual feature extraction, thereby improving the detection accuracy [29, 30]. For exam­
ple, Udo et al. [31] used machine learning to optimize wind energy systems to achieve 
predictive maintenance and improve efficiency, and further improved the accuracy of 
diagnosis by combining with traditional methods. However, deep learning models have 
high requirements on data quality and data volume, and are prone to over-fitting prob­
lems when processing high-dimensional and sparse signals [32, 33]. Therefore, how to 
efficiently collect and process signals and improve the robustness of deep learning mod­
els is still an important challenge faced by current methods [34, 35].
In view of the shortcomings of the current research field, this paper applies an innova­
tive wind turbine blade damage detection technology that integrates sparse represen­
tation, compressed sensing, and deep learning theory. First, sparse representation and 
compressed sensing methods are embedded in the technical framework to implement 
dimensional reduction and noise suppression on the sound-print signal of the wind tur­
bine blade. Subsequently, the study applies a CNN, using its powerful automatic feature 
learning ability to deeply mine and extract key information from the signal. Through this 
method, the computational complexity is greatly reduced, and the real-time response 
speed, accuracy, and intelligence of damage detection are significantly improved. The 
outcomes demonstrate that the detection strategy proposed in this paper that combines 
sparse representation, compressed sensing, and deep learning has shown excellent per­
formance improvements in multiple test cases. This technology not only has excellent 
versatility and can flexibly adapt to different application scenarios, but also shows good 
expansion potential, ensuring stable operation under different working conditions.
2  Methodology
2.1  Signal acquisition and preprocessing
To obtain the voiceprint signal of the wind turbine blade, this paper selects high-preci­
sion acoustic sensors and vibration sensors  [36, 37]. Specifically, a multi-channel micro­
phone array is used to capture the voiceprint signal generated when the fan is running 
[38]. Through the distributed arrangement of multiple microphones, the voiceprint infor­
mation from different positions and angles can be obtained. In addition, accelerometer 
and displacement sensors are installed to supplement the collection of vibration signals 
so as to obtain the dynamic features of the wind turbine blades more comprehensively. 
The microphone array is evenly arranged at different positions from the wind turbine

blades, especially in the leading edge, middle, and trailing edge areas of the fan. The spac­
ing between each microphone is about 0.5 m to ensure coverage of the entire blade area. 
The arrangement method enables the sound wave signals of the wind turbine blades to be 
captured from multiple directions and multiple distances, avoiding the information loss 
caused by a single angle. The height of the array is kept at a distance of about 2 m from the 
blade, which can accurately capture the sound waves generated by the interaction between 
air flow and the blade surface. The vibration sensors are mainly installed at the root and 
tip of the blade, which are usually greatly affected by wind speed changes and blade dam­
age. The root sensor mainly monitors the vibration features of the connection between the 
blade and the shaft, while the tip sensor focuses on the dynamic response of the blade tip 
and can capture more subtle damage signals. The accelerometer are distributed along the 
length of the blade to cover a wider monitoring range. Since the damage signals of wind 
turbine blades usually have more complex time-frequency features, it is necessary to select 
a suitable signal sampling rate to capture sufficiently delicate signal features. According to 
the frequency range of the wind turbine operation, this paper adopts a higher sampling 
rate (10 kHz) to ensure that all possible high-frequency components are captured. A sam­
pling rate that is too low may cause signal distortion, while a sampling rate that is too high 
may bring unnecessary data redundancy and increase the computational burden of sub­
sequent signal processing. A sampling rate of 10 kHz provides a balance point for wind 
blade monitoring, which can capture key frequency components while avoiding excessive 
redundant data.Each time data is collected; a time window (5 s) is set; continuous signal 
collection is performed within this time window to ensure the integrity and stability of the 
signal.

2.2  Sparse representation and feature extraction
In the damage detection process of voiceprint signals, the signal dimension is usually high 
and contains much redundant information. This redundant information not only increases 
the computational burden, but also may affect the accuracy of subsequent processing. To 
effectively extract meaningful features from high-dimensional signals and reduce data 
redundancy, this paper adopts sparse representation method for signal processing.
Figure 2 shows the combination of dictionary learning and OMP (Orthogonal Match­
ing Pursuit) algorithm to extract damage features of wind turbine blade voiceprint sig­
nals. First, a dictionary learning method is used to generate an adaptive dictionary that 
can effectively express signals under the sparse representation framework.Using the 
sparse coding method to pre-train the dictionary as initialization can obtain a better

initial representation and reduce randomness during training. The basic concept of dic­
tionary learning is to train a set of basis functions so that the sparse linear combination 
of these basis functions can approximate the acoustic signal of the wind turbine blade. 
The signal is specifically represented as a sparse linear combination of the dictionary, 
which means that each signal segment has a sparse coefficient that is determined to 
minimize the reconstruction error. Dictionary learning gradually adjusts the dictionary 
through an iterative optimization process so that each signal sample can be efficiently 
expressed by a combination of a small number of basis elements, thereby effectively 
extracting the main features in the signal. After the dictionary learning is completed, 
the L1 norm minimization algorithm, especially the orthogonal matching pursuit algo­
rithm, is utilized to select sparse features related to the damage features from the origi­
nal signal. The OMP algorithm iteratively selects the most relevant elements in the 
dictionary and gradually builds a sparse representation of the signal according to the size 
of the residual. Each time, the dictionary element that can best reduce the residual is 
selected, and the residual is updated until the predetermined sparsity requirement or 
error threshold is reached. In this way, OMP can extract the most representative features 
from the original signal, thereby avoiding the redundancy problem of high-dimensional 
features in traditional methods, significantly reducing the dimension of the signal, and 
retaining sufficient signal information. In practical applications, to enable OMP to effec­
tively process the noise and unstable components in the voiceprint signal, this paper 
controls the accuracy of the sparse representation by setting appropriate thresholds and 
stopping criteria. Specifically, the coefficient value of the dictionary element selected by 
the OMP algorithm each time exceeds a certain threshold and is included in the calcula­
tion, avoiding the application of too many irrelevant components. Through this process, 
the OMP algorithm can automatically recognize and extract signal features related to 
wind turbine blade damage, significantly improving the sparsity of signal representation 
and the selectivity of features.The number of OMP iterations is fifty, and it stops when 
the maximum number of iterations is reached.
To optimize the effect of sparse representation, this study integrates the local diction­
ary learning method. This method allows learning exclusive dictionaries for different 
sections of the signal, so that the voiceprint features of the wind turbine blades under 
different operating conditions can be captured more precisely. When constructing each 
local dictionary, the uniqueness of the local area of the signal is fully considered, so that 
the dictionary elements are highly consistent with the local feature distribution of the 
signal, thereby enhancing the representation accuracy and robustness of the signal. After 
sparse representation processing, the obtained signal features are both compressed and 
representative, and can effectively retain information directly related to the damage of 
the wind turbine blades while reducing the signal dimension. This process avoids the 
problem of information loss or high computational complexity caused by signal redun­
dancy in traditional signal processing methods, and provides a more precise and concise 
data basis for subsequent signal analysis and deep learning model training.
In addition, to further improve the efficiency of feature extraction, the study also inte­
grates a multi-scale feature extraction strategy. When multi-scale feature fusion, fea­
tures can be combined by weighted average, and the weight coefficient is optimized by 
grid search to ensure that the contribution of each scale feature in the final decision is 
optimized. By fusing features at multiple scales, the model’s ability to recognize various

2.3  Compressed sensing and data compression
In the damage detection process of wind turbine blade voiceprint signals, signal acquisi­
tion and storage usually require a lot of resources. Especially when the signal dimension 
is high, the data volume is huge, which brings great storage and transmission pressure. To 
efficiently reduce the amount of data and retain the useful information in the original sig­
nal as much as possible, this paper adopts compressed sensing technology to compress 
and reconstruct the signal.
First, an appropriate sampling matrix is chosen to compress the signal. To achieve 
effective compressed sensing, it is first necessary to construct a sampling matrix that 
matches the sparsity of the signal. A random sampling matrix, such as a Gaussian ran­
dom matrix or a Bernoulli matrix, is used to linearly sample the signal. These matrices 
can reduce the number of samples by randomly selecting sampling points without los­
ing the key information of the signal. The Gaussian matrix has good theoretical perfor­
mance and can better restore sparse signals. Generating and storing Gaussian matrices 
requires more computing resources and has low computational efficiency, especially in 
high-dimensional data. The Bernoulli matrix has high storage and computational effi­
ciency and is simple to generate and apply. For some complex sparse signals, the Ber­
noulli matrix may not be able to efficiently preserve the sparsity characteristics of the 
signal, resulting in slightly lower reconstruction accuracy. Choose a Gaussian random 
matrix. Although it has a large computational and storage overhead, it has high stability 
and accuracy in signal reconstruction, especially in high-dimensional sparse signals.
After the signal is compressed and sampled, compressed data with a dimension far 
lower than the original signal is obtained. These compressed data still retain the main 
features of the signal and have high sparsity. According to the theory of compressed 
sensing, under certain conditions, the compressed signal can be accurately recon­
structed with fewer sample points. To recover the original signal from the compressed 
data, this paper adopts an optimization algorithm based on sparse reconstruction. Com­
mon methods include algorithms based on L1 norm minimization, such as the total vari­
ation minimization algorithm, and algorithms based on iterative reconstruction, such as 
matching pursuit and basis pursuit. In the specific implementation process, the signal 
is first reconstructed through the L1 norm minimization problem. The core idea of L1 
norm minimization is to minimize the error between the reconstructed signal and the 
original signal while maintaining the signal sparsity. Specifically, the signal reconstruc­
tion process is expressed as:

the number of sampling points, greatly reducing the cost of data collection and storage, 
while also reducing the burden of data transmission. In addition, the reconstructed sig­
nal of the compressed sensing method can retain enough important information, laying 
a solid foundation for feature extraction and damage detection.
In practical applications, this study verifies the effectiveness of the compressed sens­
ing method in the voiceprint signals of wind turbine blades through simulation experi­
ments. The experimental results show that compressed sensing technology can recover 
signals with high similarity to the original signals at a much lower sampling rate than the 
standard method. This not only reduces the pressure of data storage and transmission, 
but also improves the efficiency of data processing. At the same time, in the case of large 
noise, compressed sensing can still effectively extract useful features of the signal, ensur­
ing the accuracy of signal reconstruction.The dictionary learning algorithm optimizes 
the signal reconstruction error by iteratively updating the dictionary and sparse coef­
ficient matrix. The dictionary update uses the method of minimizing the reconstruction 
error and regularization to ensure that the dictionary adapts to the signal characteris­
tics. The dictionary that is robust to noise can improve noise tolerance through weighted 
least squares or L1 regularization.
The compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction process is highly sensitive to changes in

2.4  Deep learning model and damage recognition
In the task scope of wind turbine blade damage detection, sparse representation and com­
pressed sensing technologies have effectively helped signal data noise reduction, dimen­
sional reduction and compression processing. However, precisely extracting high-level 
features closely related to damage from these pre-processed signals and classifying and 
locating them based on them is still a core problem that needs to be addressed urgently. In 
response to this challenge, this study applies CNNs to enhance the ability of feature extrac­
tion and damage recognition.
Specifically, the voiceprint signals of wind turbine blades after sparse representation 
are used as input data of the CNN model. Thanks to the pre-processing of sparse rep­
resentation and compressed sensing technology, these signals already contain sparse 
features related to damage, and the dimensions are significantly reduced, making them 
more suitable for the training needs of DL models. To maximize the effectiveness of 
CNN, the input format of the signal needs to match the network structure. To realize 
the network’s autonomous learning of the spatial structure information of the signal, the 
processed signal is specially reshaped into a two-dimensional matrix form suitable for 
CNN convolution operations. This ensures that CNN can efficiently mine and utilize the 
deep features in the signal, laying a solid foundation for subsequent damage recognition 
and classification.
The CNN model uses multi-layer convolution operations to extract signal features 
layer by layer. The network uses the local receptive field in the first convolutional layer 
to extract low-level features such as edges and textures. The convolution kernel (7 × 7) 
is suitable for capturing global features and is suitable for detecting larger damage. The 
step size = 1 retains more details and is suitable for fine damage identification.Through 
layer-by-layer processing of activation functions, pooling, and convolution, these low-
level information are converted into more abstract high-level features. For example, 
through multiple convolution and pooling operations, the network can recognize high-
order information such as frequency and amplitude related to the damage pattern in the 
signal. In the convolution operation of each layer, ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) is uti­
lized to enhance the effectiveness of feature extraction.
The next pooling layer processes the features extracted by the convolution layer. The 
role of the pooling layer is to minimize the amount of computation, retain important fea­
ture information, and reduce the dimensionality of the data through the down-sampling

the network enters the fully connected layer, which is mainly responsible for further 
processing and classification of the collected high-level attributes. The fully connected 
layer uses weighted summation to combine the features obtained from the multi-layer 
convolution process and output the damage probability for each category. To prevent

2.5  Multi-level fusion and optimization
To further enhance the accuracy and robustness of wind turbine blade damage detection, 
this paper combines the long short-term memory (LSTM) network on the basis of the 
CNN to enhance the detection ability of dynamic damage to wind turbine blades. Spe­
cifically, CNN is mainly utilized to extract the spatial features of the signal, while LSTM 
is mainly responsible for analyzing the changes in the signal in the time dimension. The 
combination of the two can effectively enhance the recognition accuracy of the model for 
dynamic and complex damage patterns.
First, the features extracted in the CNN network are processed by convolution and 
pooling to form a high-level abstract representation of the signal. However, the damage 
of wind turbine blades is usually dynamic. Especially under different working conditions, 
the manifestation of damage may change over time. Therefore, relying solely on the spa­
tial features extracted by CNN is not enough to fully capture these dynamically changing 
information. To solve this problem, this paper applies the LSTM network to enhance the 
network’s processing capabilities in the time dimension. The LSTM network is a recur­
rent neural network that is good at processing time series data. Its internal gating mech­
anism can effectively capture the changes of signals over time, thereby extracting the 
time-dependent features of the signal.
In terms of network structure design, the features extracted by the CNN module are first 
flattened into a one-dimensional vector as the input of the LSTM. The LSTM layer pro­
cesses these time series features to capture the temporal dynamic changes of the signal. For 
example, for the damage signal of the wind turbine blade, the initiation, development, and 
expansion of the damage usually have obvious time features. LSTM can effectively recog­
nize the key points in these time series and respond to the dynamic changes in the signal.
Serial fusion can enhance LSTM’s ability to extract dynamic damage features, especially 
in learning long-term dependencies and changing trends. Through the high-level features 
extracted by CNN, LSTM can more effectively capture the complex time series patterns in 
damage development.
To further optimize the performance of the network, this paper adopts a multi-layer 
stacking structure in the LSTM network. Multi-layer LSTM can learn complex time 
series features at a higher level and improve the network’s ability to model long-term 
dependencies. For example, when detecting certain types of wind turbine blade damage, 
the impact of the damage may only gradually appear after a certain period of time. The 
multi-layer LSTM network can capture these long-term dependencies, thereby enhanc­
ing the detection accuracy.
Figure 4 shows the time series signal and how LSTM extracts the key time points of 
damage from it. Under normal conditions, the signal waveform is relatively stable, but 
abnormal fluctuations occur at specific moments, indicating potential damage. The posi­
tion marked by the red dot indicates the point where the damage occurs. At this time, 
the amplitude of the signal has changed significantly, which may be caused by micro-
cracks, slight wear, or other initial damage on the blade. The position marked by the 
green dot represents the development point of the damage, at which time the cracks 
extend, the wear increases, or other damage intensifies. The position marked by the pur­
ple dot is the extension point of the damage, at which time the damage has significantly 
affected the structure of the wind turbine blade, and the signal features have changed 
significantly.

Furthermore, considering that the damage pattern of the wind turbine blade may show 
different features at different time scales, this paper also applies a bidirectional LSTM 
in the LSTM network. The bidirectional LSTM further enhances the model’s ability to 
understand the time series features by considering the past and future information of 
the signal. In the bidirectional LSTM, the signal is not only processed by the forward 
LSTM network, but also processed in reverse by the reverse LSTM network. Finally, the 
forward and reverse output results are spliced to obtain more comprehensive time series 
information. Through this two-way processing method, the network can better capture 
the complex dynamic changes of the signal. Especially when the signal shows different 
change trends after the damage occurs, it can provide more precise diagnostic results.
This study uses the Dropout regularization technique during training to further 
enhance the model’s generalization ability. By randomly removing a portion of neurons 
from the LSTM layer after each training, dropout can prevent the model from over-
fitting and improve its performance on unrecognized data. Specifically, the network 
randomly selects a portion of neurons to discard at each time step of the LSTM layer, 
thereby enhancing the model and preventing over-reliance on any one neuron. Observe 
the performance of the training and validation sets under each configuration and find a 
balance point that can meet the model performance requirements without over-fitting 
or computational bottlenecks.

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed wind turbine blade dam­
age detection method, this paper conducts a detailed evaluation from multiple aspects,

3.1  Damage classification accuracy
Damage classification accuracy measures the model’s ability to accurately distinguish dif­
ferent types of wind turbine blade damage. Since there may be many different types of 
damage (such as cracks, corrosion, deformation, etc.), the accuracy of damage classifica­
tion is crucial. In the experiments, the proposed method has higher classification accuracy 
than traditional methods and single CNN methods on multiple damage categories, espe­
cially when dealing with complex dynamic damage patterns.
The X-axis of Fig. 5 lists five common types of wind turbine blade damage, and the 
Y-axis represents classification accuracy. This method shows a high classification accu­
racy of no less than 88% for all damage types, especially in complex damage modes such 
as cracks, deformations, and impacts. The accuracy performance is greater than the tra­
ditional feature extraction-based SVM (Support Vector Machine) method and the single 
CNN method. The feature extraction-based SVM method performs poorly under some 
damage types. Especially when dealing with corrosion and fatigue damage, its accuracy 
is low, reflecting the insufficient adaptability of traditional methods to complex damage.
3.2  Computational efficiency
In the practical application of wind turbine blade damage detection, computational effi­
ciency is a factor that cannot be ignored, especially in the monitoring scenario of large-
scale wind turbine groups. The method in this paper reduces the burden of data acquisition

sparse representation and compressed sensing technology. In addition, the deep learning 
model is combined for feature extraction and damage recognition, and the efficient convo­
lution and LSTM network structure is adopted to ensure that the wind turbine blade dam­
age detection task can be completed quickly while ensuring high accuracy.

4  Discussion
The wind power blade damage detection method proposed in this study, which integrates 
sparse representation, compressed sensing, and deep learning techniques, demonstrates 
significant advantages in terms of accuracy (≥ 88%), timeliness (≤ 0.45s), and resource 
adaptability. In contrast to the traditional vibration detection method that exhibits a 15% 
false positive rate, the proposed approach achieves a breakthrough through a three-stage 
collaborative mechanism: sparse coding eliminates 60% of redundant voice print features; 
compressed sensing reduces data acquisition requirements by 70% (RMSE < 0.12); and 
convolutional neural networks (CNN) automatically extract multi-scale spatiotemporal 
damage features to effectively mitigate complex environmental interference.
However, current methods still face some challenges. Notably, in the sparse represen­
tation stage, the orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) algorithm, which accounts for 65% 
of the computational time, constitutes a major bottleneck. To address this issue, several 
strategies can be explored. First, parallel acceleration techniques can be applied to cer­
tain steps of the OMP process, such as the parallel evaluation of candidate dictionary 
atoms and the parallel computation of residuals and sparse coefficients. Second, approx­
imate sparse methods, such as approximate message passing (AMP) or gradient pursuit 
algorithms, can be adopted to achieve faster convergence while maintaining acceptable 
sparse representation accuracy. Third, optimizing the dictionary structure and using 
adaptive sparsity control can help reduce the number of iterations required for OMP. 
Additionally, hardware acceleration techniques such as GPUs or FPGAs can be utilized 
to accelerate the OMP algorithm. Finally, combining OMP with other sparse representa­
tion algorithms or applying preprocessing and dimensional reduction techniques to the 
signal before OMP can also improve computational efficiency. It is worth noting that 
while these optimization methods can enhance OMP’s computational efficiency, they 
may introduce trade-offs, such as a slight decrease in sparse representation accuracy or 
increased implementation complexity. Therefore, the choice of optimization strategy 
should be based on the specific requirements and constraints of the actual application.
The implementation of distributed sensor configurations along with compatibility for 
edge computing offers an economical solution for retrofitting older wind farms, with 
microphone arrays costing only 20% of traditional acoustic monitoring systems. Cur­
rent limitations primarily stem from laboratory data exhibiting environmental bias and 
the orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) algorithm accounting for 65% of computational 
time. Future improvements will focus on adaptive threshold optimization to address 
noise reduction attenuation under a signal-to-noise ratio below 30 dB as well as hard­
ware acceleration strategies.
It is noteworthy that this method has achieved an accuracy rate of 82% in detecting 
cracks in aircraft wings, thereby validating its feasibility for cross-field applications. 
Looking ahead, efforts will concentrate on promoting multi-modal data fusion, enhanc­
ing explainable AI through attention mechanism visualization, and advancing transfer 
learning research to expedite the transition from laboratory results to industrial scenar­
ios such as offshore wind power generation.

5  Conclusion
This study adopts a wind turbine blade damage recognition method that combines deep 
learning, compressed sensing, and sparse representation to enhance the accuracy and real-
time performance of wind turbine blade damage diagnosis. CNNs and LSTM networks 
enhance the model’s robustness and the damage pattern recognition accuracy; compressed 
sensing technology reduces the amount of data collection and storage requirements; 
sparse representation methods effectively extract key information from wind turbine blade 
voiceprint signals and remove redundant data. Experimental results show that this method 
is superior to existing deep learning models and traditional technologies regarding accu­
racy and real-time performance, and also greatly improves the computational efficiency 
and damage detection accuracy.
However, although the proposed method has achieved excellent results in many evalu­
ation indicators, there are still challenges in data quality and model generalization abil­
ity. In the future, the optimization direction of multi-modal fusion feature learning, data 
quality optimization, and model training for different types of wind turbine blade dam­
age can be the key to further improving model performance and application scope.

Abstract: In view of the problem that the high noise and data redundancy in the voiceprint signal of the wind turbine blade lead to insufficient diagnostic accuracy and real- time performance and increase the acquisition cost, this paper combines sparse representation, compressed sensing, and deep learning technology to apply a new wind turbine blade damage detection method, aiming to enhance the accuracy and real-time performance of wind turbine blade damage diagnosis. The sparse representation method is used to effectively encode the voiceprint signal and extract representative signal features; the compressed sensing technology is applied to efficiently reconstruct the signal using a small amount of sampled data, significantly reducing the data collection amount and storage requirements; deep feature learning and damage pattern classification based on convolutional neural network further improve the accuracy and intelligence level of detection.The research results show that the proposed method effectively reduces the computational complexity and greatly improves the detection accuracy. The accuracy is not less than 88% under five damage types: crack, corrosion, deformation, fatigue and impact. It has good adaptability under different computing resources, and the processing delay does not exceed 0.45s under complex environments and large data volumes. It has strong real-time performance and application potential. Highlights • Innovative Fusion Approach: Combines sparse representation for feature encoding, compressed sensing for efficient data reconstruction, and deep learning (CNN) for intelligent damage classification, enhancing accuracy and real- time performance in blade damage detection. • High Accuracy & Efficiency: Achieves ≥ 88% accuracy across five damage types (crack, corrosion, deformation, fatigue, impact) with processing delays ≤ 0.45s, even in complex environments and large datasets. • Resource Adaptability: Demonstrates robust performance under varying computational resources, reducing data acquisition/storage costs while maintaining reliability in noisy, high-redundancy signal environments.
